title: Tina: Tiny Reasoning Models via LoRA
one_liner: You can teach a tiny language model to reason step-by-step cheaply by freezing most weights and tweaking only a small side adapter with reinforcement learning.
lead: Teaching language models to reason—to work through problems step by step instead of guessing—usually costs thousands of dollars in computing power. Tina shows you can do it on a 1.5 billion parameter model (tiny by today's standards) for just $9 by using a trick called LoRA: freeze the base model's weights and train only a small low-rank adapter instead. The paper's real finding is that this works because reinforcement learning for reasoning doesn't need the model to learn new facts, just to learn the format of good step-by-step thinking.

paras: Teaching a language model to reason—to show its work instead of just blurting an answer—is hard because you need to train on step-by-step thinking traces. These traces come from much larger, smarter models. The training usually runs on expensive graphics cards for days or weeks, costing thousands of dollars in electricity and hardware rental.

A naive person might try this: take a tiny model and just run full-parameter training on it, updating every single weight in the model as you teach it the reasoning format. That works, but it is wasteful—you are tuning weights that already know how to read English and do basic math. What you really need is just the bones of how to write a step-by-step proof.

callout.html: Updating every weight in a tiny model to teach it to reason wastes compute on knowledge it already has, making the whole process much more expensive than it needs to be.

steps.b: Start with a pretrained tiny model
steps.text: Load a 1.5B parameter model that already knows language and math.
Lock down the model's original weights so they do not change.
Add a small learnable side-module that can twist the model's thinking without rewriting it.

steps.b: Run reinforcement learning on the adapter only
steps.text: Show the model reasoning examples. Reward format and accuracy. Let the adapter learn what adjustments produce good step-by-step thinking.

steps.b: Stop early, use the best checkpoint
steps.text: The best model shows up after just 20-50% of one training epoch. Stop there, do not keep training.

paras: The paper changes which part of the model you train during reinforcement learning. Normally you would update all the weights in the model. Tina freezes the base model and trains only a small low-rank adapter—a compact side-module that applies small adjustments on top of the frozen base.

hidden.name: Format reward
paras: The paper measures format reward: a score that tracks how well the model outputs step-by-step reasoning in the expected structure (like Show your work, Step 1, Step 2, etc.), separate from whether the answer is correct. Think of it as grading the skeleton of reasoning, not the final answer.

During training, the reinforcement learning agent watches format reward grow quickly—the model learns the structure in just the first 200-400 training steps. Then format reward flattens out. Meanwhile, raw accuracy reward comes later and more slowly. This tells the researchers that LoRA is doing something different than full training: it learns the reasoning format first, then accuracy, while base knowledge sits unchanged. The paper shows this by plotting format reward over training steps and seeing the sharp rise, turnaround, and plateau.

heat.caption: Darker cells show where action happens: format reward spikes early (steps 1-200), then plateaus while accuracy rises slowly. Best model before step 500. Marks highlight the turning point.

reads.html: The model learns to write down its thinking step-by-step. We measure how well it does that before we even check if the answer is right. If that score goes up fast and then flattens, it means the model is learning format, not struggling to rewire its knowledge.

Format reward tracks model compliance with the RL-desired output structure. Its rapid rise and plateau in early training, decoupled from accuracy growth, support the hypothesis that LoRA learns format structure while preserving base model knowledge, in contrast to full-parameter training which integrates knowledge and format simultaneously.

paras: The mechanism works in three steps. First, LoRA computes its updates as low-rank matrix products—roughly, two thin matrices multiplied together to make a small weight change. This is much faster to compute than updating full weight matrices. Second, by freezing the base model, you skip the most expensive part of training: letting the model relearn language and math from the reasoning examples. The base already knows those; you only need to wire up the reasoning format on top. Third, reinforcement learning for reasoning rewards a specific format (work shown step-by-step), and that format can be learned by a small adapter. The adapter does not need to change every weight—it just needs to steer the model toward that structure.

The paper shows this by comparing training cost (number of math operations) against reasoning accuracy. Full-parameter models need millions of operations to hit the same accuracy. LoRA models hit it in thousands. Moreover, the best model often appears at only 20-50% through one epoch of training. If you kept training, accuracy would actually drop—a sign the adapter has already learned the format and continuing just makes it forget, because the reward signal for format stabilizes early, and pushing the adapter further only distorts the frozen base model's outputs beyond the point where the reasoning structure stays clean.

stages.s: Math problem: solve and show all work, step by step.
Base model reads problem (frozen, already knows English and math)
Adapter steers output toward Step-one, Step-two, Step-three format
Reward signal checks: Did it show work? Is answer correct?
Only adapter gets nudged by the reward direction. Base untouched.
Reasoning output, format clean, base knowledge preserved intact.

math.words: Each adapter update is a low-rank product: change equals two thin matrices multiplied, scaled by how much the reinforcement learning reward improved.
symbols: the weight change in the LoRA adapter
how big a step to take when updating (set beforehand, e.g. 0.01)
which direction to nudge to increase reward (from reinforcement learning)
a thin matrix of rank r (e.g. 8 rows, 100 columns)
another thin matrix (e.g. 100 columns, width of model layer)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the base model's weight W is 100 rows by 100 columns (10,000 numbers). Full training would update all 10,000.
LoRA instead uses A (100 by 8) and B (8 by 100). Total: 800 + 800 = 1,600 numbers.
Each step, reward_gradient tells us which direction to nudge. Learning rate is 0.01. A sample signal strength is 0.5.
For one layer: delta = 0.01 * 0.5 * (A @ B) = 0.005 * (A @ B), a 100-by-100 change.
That one update, applied to the adapter, costs roughly 1,600 multiplies. Full training would cost 10,000 multiplies. LoRA is 6x faster per step.
Over 400 training steps, LoRA trains in hours. Full training would take a day. Times 10 seeds, 20 dataset variations, and it is thousands of dollars vs. nine dollars.

math.note: The product A @ B is small because A and B are thin (low rank), so updating the adapter is much cheaper than updating the full weight matrix W.

bars.h2: LoRA vs. full training on tiny models

charts.title: Full-parameter training
charts.note: Every weight updates. Slow. Expensive. Wasteful on frozen knowledge.

charts.title: Tina with LoRA
charts.note: Only adapter updates. Format learned early. Base knowledge preserved. 30x faster, 30x cheaper, better accuracy, because the adapter learns the format structure in the first 200 training steps, then stops improving—no need to keep paying for compute—while the frozen base model already carries all the language and math knowledge, so no waste on relearning.

items.b: Training too long kills the model.
items.html: If you train beyond the turning point (after 20-50% of one epoch), the adapter starts overfitting. Accuracy drops. Format reward flattens and inverts. The model forgets how to reason. Solution: monitor format reward and stop early.

items.b: LoRA rank too small, adapter cannot learn.
items.html: If A and B are too thin (rank too low, say rank 2), the adapter has too few knobs to steer the model. Reasoning accuracy plateaus early. Solution: use rank 8 or higher for reasoning tasks.

items.b: Wrong reasoning datasets waste the training.
items.html: RL only works if the dataset has clear right and wrong answers. If examples are ambiguous or wrong, the reward signal is noise. The adapter learns garbage. Solution: use verified reasoning datasets (math, code) with clear ground truth.

items.b: Done right: frozen base, low-rank adapter, clean RL reward, early stopping.
items.html: The method works when all three pieces align: base knowledge locked down and trusted, adapter lean and fast, reward signal clear and verifiable. On math reasoning, this gives 43% accuracy for $9.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should build a tiny reasoning model (start with a 1.5B or 2B pretrained language model), add a LoRA adapter (rank 8, 2% of base weights), and run a simple reinforcement learning loop on a clean reasoning dataset. Track three metrics over training: (1) format reward (does the output match Show-your-work structure?), (2) accuracy (do the answers match the ground truth?), and (3) training cost (wall-clock time, GPU memory, FLOPs). The demo should prove that format reward spikes early, then accuracy rises more slowly, and the best checkpoint is well before epoch end. The visible proof is the chart: format reward rises in a steep curve and flattens by step 300, while accuracy is still rising at step 1000.
demo.metric_eq: Reasoning accuracy = (correct answers on held-out math problems) / (total problems); training cost = GPU hours * GPU rental price per hour; format reward = (outputs matching expected structure) / (total outputs)
demo.closing: The demo must show the chart of format vs. accuracy reward over training steps. That one chart proves the mechanism: LoRA learns structure first (format reward high, early, plateaued), preserves base knowledge (no retraining needed), and stops paying for extra steps (best model at 30% epoch completion, not 100%).
